notes.meaning: In the first month of their fortieth year in the desert, Israel arrives at Kadesh in the Wilderness of Zin. Miriam dies there and is buried. Her death reminds the people that the older generation is passing away, exactly as the Lord had said.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Some Catholic writers saw Miriam as a picture of the Virgin Mary, pointing to her unmarried life and her leadership among the women of Israel.

notes.meaning: The camp runs out of water, so the people gather to confront Moses and Aaron. Even after decades of seeing God provide, the community panics as soon as the land is dry. It is easy to forget God's past faithfulness whenever a new trial arrives.

The people argue bitterly with Moses. They wish they had died alongside their relatives who fell earlier under the Lord's judgment. Instead of praying for help, this new generation repeats the angry complaints of their parents.

The crowd asks why Moses and Aaron brought the Lord's assembly into this wasteland just to die with their animals. They speak as if their leaders led them out on purpose to destroy them. Fear can lead people to blame others instead of seeking the Lord.

The people complain about leaving Egypt for an uncomfortable place with no grain, figs, grapes, pomegranates, or water. They focus only on what the desert lacks and forget the cruel slavery they left behind. A complaining heart often misremembers the past.

Moses and Aaron leave the shouting crowd, go to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting, and fall face down. As they pray, the bright glory of the Lord appears to them. Taking our problems straight to God is always the best first move in a crisis.

The Lord tells Moses to take the staff from the tabernacle and gather the whole congregation with Aaron. God instructs them to speak directly to the rock in front of everyone, promising that water will pour out for the people and their animals. God gives simple, gracious directions to meet their physical need.
Moses obeys God's command and takes the staff from the Lord's presence in the tabernacle. This staff was kept before the Ark as a symbol of God's power and authority.

Moses and Aaron gather the community in front of the rock, but Moses speaks out of anger. He calls the people rebels and asks if he and Aaron must fetch them water from the rock. Instead of quietly giving God the glory, Moses lets his temper make it sound like the leaders perform the miracle.

Moses raises his hand and strikes the rock twice with his staff instead of just speaking to it. Even though Moses disobeyed in anger, water gushes out in abundance so that the people and their herds can drink. God remains merciful to His thirsty people even when His servants fail.

The Lord rebukes Moses and Aaron because they did not trust Him or honor His holiness before the Israelites. Because of this public failure, God announces that neither brother will lead the assembly into the Promised Land. God holds leaders to high standards because their words and actions show His character to others.

differ.view: Some evangelicals teach that striking the rock twice ruined a prophetic picture of Christ, who was to be struck only once on the cross and then approached through prayer.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic commentary notes that Moses and Aaron showed a weakness of faith by relying on a previously successful method rather than following God's new direction, though without losing God's overall favor.

notes.meaning: The place is called the waters of Meribah, which means quarreling, because Israel argued with the Lord there. God demonstrated His holiness by providing fresh water and by holding Moses and Aaron accountable.

Moses sends messengers from Kadesh to the king of Edom, calling Israel his brother and recounting all their hardships. Because the Edomites descended from Esau and the Israelites from Jacob, Moses appeals to their family ties for safe passage.

The messengers explain how Israel's ancestors moved to Egypt and lived there for centuries until the Egyptians mistreated them. Moses shares this painful history to ask for kindness from their distant relatives.

The message tells how the Lord heard Israel's cry of misery, sent an angel to lead them out of Egypt, and brought them to Kadesh on Edom's border. Moses points to God's rescue as the reason they are asking for a peaceful passage.

Israel asks for permission to pass through Edom, promising not to cut through fields, harm vineyards, or drink from private wells. They pledge to stay strictly on the King's Highway, the main royal road, until they cross the border. Respecting the property of others is an important part of peaceable living.
The king of Edom flatly refuses the request and threatens to attack Israel with an army if they try to cross the land. Fear and old grudges keep Edom from showing mercy to their relatives.

The Israelites reply that they will stay entirely on the main highway and pay in full for any water they or their livestock drink. They emphasize that they only wish to pass through on foot without causing any damage.
Edom repeats the refusal and marches out a large, heavily armed army to guard the boundary. The king chooses military force and suspicion over peaceful cooperation.

Faced with Edom's armed refusal, Israel turns away instead of forcing a fight. God had commanded them not to war against their brother nation, so they patiently chose a longer route around the border.
The entire assembly leaves Kadesh and arrives at Mount Hor on the border of Edom. God preserved the whole camp through the standoff so that not a single person was harmed.
At Mount Hor, near the edge of Edom, the Lord speaks to Moses and Aaron. God prepares the two brothers for Aaron's life and ministry to come to an end.

The Lord announces that Aaron will die and be gathered to his people without entering the Promised Land. This judgment comes because both brothers disobeyed God's command at the waters of Meribah. Even God's closest servants must face the earthly results of their mistakes.
God directs Moses to bring Aaron and his son Eleazar up Mount Hor away from the camp. This quiet ascent gives Aaron time to prepare for death in the presence of his brother and son.

God instructs Moses to remove Aaron's holy priestly garments and place them on Eleazar, where Aaron will die. Transferring the robes confirms that Eleazar is now the high priest and that God's priesthood will continue without interruption.

Moses carries out the Lord's orders, and the three men climb Mount Hor before the eyes of the entire community. The whole camp watches as their first high priest walks up the mountain for the last time.

Moses removes Aaron's priestly robes and puts them on Eleazar, and Aaron dies peacefully on top of the mountain. Moses and Eleazar then walk down together, closing Aaron's forty years of service. Human leaders pass away, but the ministry of the Lord continues.

When the congregation learns that Aaron has died, the entire house of Israel mourns for him for thirty days. The people put aside their past grievances to show deep respect and honor for their departed high priest.
